c.tagline: The Capital of the Alps — a flat, mountain-ringed student city that's France's springboard to the peaks.

taxi.fareNote: Official taxis are metered with a ~€2.50 flag-fall and ~€1.90/km; find them at ranks (Gare, Place Victor-Hugo) or book by phone/app. Uber and Bolt also operate.

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU-wide emergency number and works from any phone; in France, 15 reaches the SAMU medical service and 17 the police. 18 reaches the fire brigade.

hood_landmark.Notre-Dame: Grenoble Notre-Dame cathedral square old town

avoid.reason: Caution around the station and some peripheral districts (Villeneuve) at night

hood_desc: Grenoble's flat, walkable Hyper-Centre packs pedestrian streets, big squares (Place Grenette, Place Victor-Hugo), shops and the Quai Stéphane-Jay where the 'Les Bulles' bubble cable car climbs to the Bastille fort.
The Notre-Dame quarter is the old historic heart around the cathedral and the excellent Musée de Grenoble, all cobbled lanes, terraces and the Isère riverfront beneath the mountains.
Championnet is Grenoble's bohemian, creative corner: independent boutiques, galleries, cafés, record and tattoo shops and a relaxed, arty daytime buzz.
Chorier-Berriat is the young, lively former industrial district by the Drac, full of bars, restaurants, live-music venues and student energy, especially after dark.
Île Verte is a quiet, leafy riverside area along the Isère with Alpine views, greenery and a calmer residential feel just east of the center.

water.note: Tap water is Alpine-sourced and safe to drink.

transit.hours: ~5:00 AM to ~1:00 AM (main tram lines run to ~2:00 AM on Fri/Sat nights)
transit.note: The TAG / M network (run by SMMAG) has 5 tram lines (A-E) and 50+ bus lines, plus 22 park-and-ride lots. The compact, flat center is very walkable and bike-friendly.
transit.pay: Single ticket €1.60 (1-hour, round trips allowed); 10 rides €13.20; day pass €4.50. Buy at tram-stop machines, tobacconists or via the app; validate on board.

bus: FlixBus and BlaBlaCar Bus coaches to Lyon, Paris, Marseille and beyond from the Gare Routière
train: Gare de Grenoble: TGV to Paris (~3h), frequent trains to Lyon (~1h15), plus TER to Chambéry, Valence and Alpine valleys

transit.m: Seasonal Transaltitude/ski shuttle to Grenoble bus station (~45 min, mainly winter weekends)
Taxi to city center (~40-45 min; GNB is 40 km out and mostly seasonal low-cost flights)
Most travelers fly into Lyon-Saint-Exupéry (LYS, ~90 km/1h drive); direct FlixBus/BlaBlaCar coach to Grenoble (~1h05, ~€19)

tip.r: ~5-10% for good service (service is included by law, 'service compris')

food.name: Gratin dauphinois
food.desc: Thinly sliced potatoes baked slowly in garlic-rubbed cream and milk until the top browns; no cheese, and the Dauphine will tell you so.

places.name: La Table Ronde
places.note: Trading since 1739 and one of the oldest restaurants in France; Alpine classics done straight.

places.name: Le Gratin Dauphinois

food.desc: Postage-stamp pasta squares filled with fresh cheese and parsley, served in cream, gratineed, or floated in broth; eaten by the dozen.

food.name: Noix de Grenoble
food.desc: The protected Grenoble walnut, sold fresh in autumn and baked into gateau aux noix, walnut tarts and oil pressed at local mills.

places.name: Halles Sainte-Claire

places.name: Marche de l'Estacade

places.name: Le Mont Rachais
places.note: Regional kitchen where walnuts turn up in salads and desserts.

food.name: Murcon
food.desc: Trieves pork sausage flavoured with fennel and caraway, poached and served hot with potatoes; a mountain winter dish rarely found elsewhere.

places.name: Le Mont Rachais

food.desc: Small, soft cow's-milk cheese from the Isere that turns almost liquid when ripe; often baked in its pot and poured over toast or potatoes.

places.name: La Table Ronde

food.name: Gateau aux noix
food.desc: Dense walnut cake or tart made with Grenoble nuts and often caramel, sold in every patisserie and taken home as the local souvenir.

places.name: Le Gratin Dauphinois

food.desc: Herbal liqueur made by Carthusian monks in the mountains north of the city, green or yellow, drunk neat over ice or in a chartreuse tonic.

landmarks: La Bastille and the Grenoble-Bastille Cable Car
Iconic glass 'bubble' gondolas float over the Isère to this 19th-century hilltop fortress, whose terraces survey the city and three mountain ranges.
Musée de Grenoble
One of France's finest art museums outside Paris pairs Rubens and Zurbarán with a stellar modern collection of Matisse, Picasso and Kandinsky.
Grenoble Old Town and Place Grenette
Café terraces and pastel facades fill the lively squares and lanes where Stendhal grew up, threaded with antique shops and walnut-cake bakeries.
Musée Dauphinois
Set in a 17th-century convent on the Bastille slopes, this engaging museum tells the Alps' human story, from mountain crafts to ski history.
Grenoble Cathedral (Notre-Dame) and Bishops' Palace Museum
The cathedral group conceals a rare 4th-century baptistery, unearthed beneath the square and displayed in the adjoining Ancien Évêché museum.
Palais du Parlement du Dauphiné
A flamboyant Gothic-Renaissance courthouse on Place Saint-André, seat of the Dauphiné's parliament for five centuries and Grenoble's handsomest facade.
Saint-Laurent Archaeological Museum
Beneath a deconsecrated church on the Isère's right bank, walkways descend through 2,000 years of crypts, tombs and Grenoble's Christian origins.
Jardin de Ville
Grenoble's oldest public garden, once Lesdiguières' private grounds, spreads plane-tree shade and pétanque beside the cable-car station.
Parc Paul Mistral and the Perret Tower
The city's great park surrounds France's first reinforced-concrete tower, an 87-metre 1925 landmark recently restored with a panoramic lift.
Fort Saint-Eynard
Perched 1,300 metres up the Chartreuse cliffs above town, this 19th-century fort delivers dizzying balcony views over Grenoble's mountain-ringed valley.

train.note: Gare de Grenoble is on the western edge of the centre, sharing its forecourt with the bus station and served by trams A and B. Direct TGVs reach Paris Gare de Lyon in about 3 hours and there are frequent TER services to Lyon (about 1h20m), Valence, Chambery and Annecy. A handful of direct trains a day continue to Geneva in around 2 hours, though most Geneva journeys involve a change at Chambery, so check whether the service you are booking is really direct. There is no rail link across the Alps to Italy from Grenoble - Turin and Milan mean changing at Chambery or Modane, and are usually quicker by coach.

intl.to: Turin, Milan, Genoa, Aosta, Florence & Rome (Italy)

bus.note: The main coach terminal is Grenoble Central Bus Station at 11 Place de la Gare, immediately next to the SNCF station, with secondary FlixBus stops at Oxford (Avenue des Martyrs) and Condillac-Universites. Grenoble is unusually well connected by international coach for its size, with direct runs to Switzerland, Italy, Spain, Germany and the Benelux. Turin is around 4 hours through the Frejus tunnel and Geneva about 2h30m. Tickets are bought online; regional ski and valley services run under the Cars Region brand and are paid for on board.

ferry.note: Grenoble sits in a mountain basin at the confluence of the Isere and the Drac, both unnavigable, so there are no ferries. The nearest scheduled passenger boats are on Lake Annecy, roughly two hours north, and Lake Geneva.

half.name: Grande Chartreuse Monastery
half.blurb: Isolated Carthusian monastery in the Chartreuse mountains where the green Chartreuse liqueur has been distilled since the 17th century.

half.name: Annecy
half.blurb: Alpine lakeside town with a turquoise lake and a canal-lined old quarter nicknamed the Venice of the Alps.

half.name: Vercors Regional Natural Park
half.blurb: Limestone plateau of gorges and forest tablelands used for hiking, caving, and Resistance history museums.

half.name: Chamrousse
half.blurb: Ski resort on the Belledonne range that hosted 1968 Olympic events, with a cable car to a panoramic Alps viewpoint.

half.name: Uriage-les-Bains
half.blurb: Thermal spa village in a wooded valley, built around 19th-century bathhouses fed by mineral springs.
